query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A tailored post‐casting heat treatment that induces the formation of coherent nanoscale precipitates at the internal lamellar boundaries in eutectic HEAs will improve both strength and room‐temperature tensile ductility relative to the as-cast continuous lamellar microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with fine lamellar dual-phase (e.g., fcc/B2) colonies featuring continuous, brittle interphase boundaries where microcracks tend to nucleate under tensile load.
generation.intervention: Apply an optimized thermal treatment (with controlled temperature, time, and cooling rate) to trigger the nucleation and growth of coherent nanoprecipitates preferentially along the lamellar boundaries without coarsening.
generation.conditions: This intervention is applicable to eutectic HEAs exhibiting fine lamellar colonies (e.g., fcc/B2 or similar dual-phase microstructures) and is effective when the heat treatment prevents precipitate coarsening and maintains phase stability. The treatment should be designed for room-temperature tensile performance.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent nanoprecipitates decorating the lamellar colony interfaces.
generation.mechanism: The formation of coherent nanoprecipitates improves yield strength by providing effective obstacles to dislocation motion and, importantly, introduces well-bonded, stress-relieving interfaces that facilitate dislocation transmission. This reduces stress concentration at the originally continuous, brittle internal boundaries, thereby mitigating microcrack initiation during tensile deformation and enhancing ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast eutectic microstructure, the treated alloy will show both an increase in tensile strength and a significant improvement in tensile ductility at room temperature.
generation.baseline: The as-cast eutectic HEA with its continuous lamellar colonies and brittle interphase boundaries that lead to premature microcracking.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of this intervention is contingent upon precise control of the heat treatment parameters. If the precipitates become too coarse or the phase stability is compromised, the improvements may not be realized. Additionally, the hypothesis applies only to alloys with eutectic lamellar microstructures under room-temperature tensile conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While prior evidence in similar alloy systems and processing strategies suggests this approach is promising, the exact quantitative improvements in strength and ductility depend on the detailed microstructural evolution, which remains to be fully characterized in eutectic HEAs.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples: a control set with the as-cast microstructure and a test set that undergoes the optimized thermal treatment aimed at inducing coherent nanoprecipitates. Carry out detailed microstructural analyses (using TEM and SEM) to verify the formation, morphology, and distribution of the precipitates. Then perform systematic room-temperature tensile tests on both sets.
measurements: TEM analysis of nanoprecipitate size, distribution, and coherence with the matrix
SEM examination of fracture surfaces to assess crack initiation and propagation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally treated samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility, or if microstructural analyses fail to show the expected coherent nanoprecipitate decorating the lamellar boundaries compared to the as-cast state, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] .
